source.title: Function-Vector Heads Are Two Populations: Writers and Cancellers in In-Context Learning

page_placements.theme: Suppressive attention heads, often working as populations, in other models and tasks
A head's signed role depends on task, readout and analysis method

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses copy suppression as related work, but its own experiments measure suppression of rule-correct answers in Pythia in-context learning, not suppression of context tokens predicted by earlier components. The related results do not test the claim versions' copy-suppression behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper cites copy suppression and discusses its relation to negative contributions. Its own measurements concern correct-versus-incorrect task-answer readouts and accuracy, not copying of earlier context tokens. Rows below record those adjacent findings as versions ["none"]. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper names copy suppression only in the introduction and in a self-repair citation. Its experiments measure 'canceller' heads in Pythia that suppress the rule-correct binary label in synthetic in-context rule tasks. It never tests whether a head suppresses context tokens predicted by earlier components. It does not study GPT-2 small L10H7, calibration, copy-suppression circuits or copy-suppression self-repair. None of its results bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that candidate function-vector heads split into writers and cancellers with opposing effects. Removing cancellers improves accuracy in all six settings, dominant suppression depends on source content, and roles change across tasks. They also stress that near-additive opposing effects can hide behind a small joint-ablation effect.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses label-sensitive DLA screening, paired interventions to assign signed roles, held-out group ablations, and source-value permutation in Pythia rule tasks. It does not apply the original copy-suppression analysis to context-token copying or GPT-2 small L10H7.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports task-dependent role changes on transfer: the hierarchical-source canceller group supports antonym answers but suppresses country-capital answers; L11.H4 supports antonym answers and has little country-capital effect.

fits_no_version.finding: In six Pythia model–rule-task settings, zero-ablating validated canceller heads raises observed accuracy by 2.4–6.8 points and the correct-label readout by +0.13 to +0.29 nats.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-sensitive heads selected from a function-vector candidate set can systematically suppress the rule-correct in-context answer, at a behavioural cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Permuting source values at fixed attention removes 52–83% of the dominant canceller's negative DLA in each setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dominant suppressive head contributions in rule tasks depend on which source content is paired with each attention weight.

fits_no_version.finding: On vocabulary tasks, the hierarchical-source canceller group and L11.H4 support antonym answers (−1.56 and −0.069 nats on ablation). The canceller groups remain suppressive on country-capital prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A head's or group's signed role (support vs suppression) depends on the task and readout.

record.problems: The main analysis covers two synthetic rule families and three Pythia models. Vocabulary transfer changes both the task and answer readout, as the authors note. Source attribution and value shuffling establish head-output-level content dependence, not a complete downstream circuit account. The study does not test copy suppression directly.
record.rows_left_out: Writer-group and joint-ablation outcomes, mean-ablation outcomes, rule-family transfer tables, and magnitude-ranking comparisons were omitted because they are not needed to record the adjacent canceller findings above; see §4.1 and Appendices B, D.1, and E. The text reports no results for the claim's copy-suppression behavior itself.

untested.parts: No GPT-2 small, no L10H7, and no test of suppressing earlier-context tokens predicted upstream across the training distribution.
No QK/OV copy-suppression circuit analysis and no fraction-of-loss explanation. The value-shuffling test concerns label-contrast DLA, not a copy-suppression mechanism.
No ablation of an upstream copier and no measure of the downstream suppression response.
Cancellers in Pythia are not tested for being copy suppressors. Their suppression of rule-correct labels is not shown to target tokens that are copied from context and predicted upstream.
No decomposition of self-repair sources. Self-repair is only cited in the discussion.

record.verdict_notes: Copy suppression is cited as related work: heads that suppress over-predicted context tokens and improve calibration. The paper does not claim its cancellers are copy suppressors. The coincidence of a Pythia-1.4B 'L10.H7' canceller has no bearing on GPT-2 small L10H7.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test GPT-2 small L10H7 or whether a head attends to earlier occurrences of tokens predicted by earlier components and suppresses them across the training distribution.
The study does not test the copy-suppression QK/OV circuit or the reported 76.9% contribution to loss.
The study does not measure calibration or naive copying.
The study does not test copy suppression as self-repair after ablation of an upstream copier.
The study does not test whether negative heads in other tasks or models implement the same copy-suppression behavior.
The study does not measure copy suppression's share of self-repair or compare it with other self-repair mechanisms.

relation.reason: Discusses copy suppression as related work in the introduction and self-repair discussion; its experiments neither test nor use the cataloged mechanism.

tranche.reason: Measures suppression of rule-correct labels, without testing suppression of earlier-context tokens predicted by upstream components, calibration, or copy-suppression self-repair.

source_check.notes: r13/r15 and r14/r18 describe the same respective interventions in different measures; do not count them as independent evidence. The authors' conclusion is accurately summarized; content-dependent negative DLA does not establish the cataloged copy-suppression mechanism.
